text: taking public-app-server/G17 -- Andy's 'joe doesn't even have a SpiritOS node' (a naming mix-up).

Right, and that's a naming mix-up on my side: I used 'joe' for two different people. Your joe is the VISITOR, a browser, no node, anonymous. My 'joe' in the A/B question was the THIRD BOX: a member with a SpiritOS node who reserved a name under your face, say carol.face.spirit.andyflinn.com. Let's call that one Carol. So the question reads: when a web request reaches Carol's node, must Carol's node refuse anything that didn't come through your appFaceApp (B), or is that simply true because Carol's node has no web port of its own (A)? The visitor never has a node either way.
taking public-app-server/G17 -- Andy's 'not needed to reach that 3rd face user'.

Understood: the third box, a member with their own node, isn't needed now, so A/B is parked. Nothing gets built for it. It goes under Open in G17 as 'members serving a face: undecided, not in scope'. Back to step 1, the route from browser to your box and back, which is built. It's waiting on the VPS setup: on-demand certificates, since the DreamHost module won't build, and the puppet node running on the VPS. That's wsl-claude's ask above.

Andy: 'it's not needed to reach that 3rd face user'. The member case is parked and A/B is dropped, so no key-check test. I'll note it under Open in G17. Step 1 stays: your lab world, plus your scripts on his go (on-demand TLS, puppet on the VPS).

Yes: the face is the browser door, the one place a browser gets in. Everything behind it is SpiritOS packets, and a member never needs a web port of their own. I'll use your word, 'browser door', in the G17 write-up.
taking public-app-server/G17 -- Andy's 'every app can kill itself and its box'.

True, and it puts the responsibility where it belongs: on the app, not the door. The face only delivers a request, bounded and named; what an app does with it is the app's own business, including foolish things. That's one question for the server-process design row: how much an app process may do to its box. Is it walled into its own folder and limits, or trusted like any program the owner installs? Your node can't stop an app from harming itself, but it can decide what an app process is allowed to reach.
Noted: what an app does to its own box is not our problem, so it stays out of the server-process design. That row covers only how a process is started, watched, and handed a request.
taking public-app-server/G17 -- Andy's 'are we clear on building ... and prove it?'

Yes, clear. BUILT (pushed): the VPS face asks your box who owns a name, remembers it, forwards the request; your box answers from grants.json and sends back 'not served yet' naming its key; the answer returns to the browser. PROOF, two parts: (1) the lab test, which wsl-claude is writing: a browser-like request for join.face.spirit.test comes back with your box's key, a second one doesn't ask again, and an unknown name gets 'no such route'. (2) Live on the VPS, which needs your one Go on wsl-claude's ask: Caddy with on-demand certificates (the DreamHost module won't build) and the puppet node running there. After that Go I add the small 'is this name granted?' check Caddy asks, and you set two things on your own box: face-domain.json and join's grant row. wsl-claude's scripts will cover both. Then you open https://join.face.spirit.andyflinn.com and see your box's key.
